Sitting at it:
Before any note, the thing that decides whether the next twenty years are comfortable.

**Height first.** Sit so that your forearms are roughly **level with the keys** — a flat line from elbow to knuckle. Too low and the wrists bend upward to reach; too high and the shoulders rise. An ordinary dining chair is usually slightly too low for a piano; a cushion fixes it.

**Distance.** Far enough back that your elbows are just in front of your body, not pinned against your sides. If you lean forward to reach the keys you are too far away; if your elbows are behind your torso you are too close.

**Sit on the front half of the bench**, feet flat on the floor, weight through the feet and the sit bones. Not slumped back — you need to be able to lean slightly into the keyboard without the chair holding you up.

**Where you sit along the keyboard.** Middle C in front of your navel — and if you do not yet know where middle C is, it is the C nearest the middle of the instrument, usually behind the lock or the maker's name on an upright. Two lessons from here you will find it by the pattern of the black keys instead of by looking. Sitting centred on the instrument gets you close enough for now.

**The shoulders are the tell.** They should hang. If they have risen towards your ears you are holding tension, and you will not notice it happening — only that your neck aches an hour later.

**Hand shape.** Let your arm hang loose by your side and look at your hand: the fingers curve naturally, the thumb falls forward, nothing is straight. That shape, lifted onto the keys, is the shape. You do not need to "hold a ball"; you need to stop flattening it.

**The acoustic matters here.** A real action has weight, so poor posture produces fatigue quickly and you will feel the feedback. That is an advantage over a light digital keyboard, where bad habits cost nothing until they cost a great deal.

**Practice.** Sit, set the height, and put your hands on the keys without playing. Check: forearms level, shoulders down, fingers curved, feet flat. Do that before every session for a month and it will stop needing checking.
How the arm makes the sound:
The single most useful thing to understand before playing a note: **the sound comes from the arm, not the finger.**

Press a key with just the finger, wrist held stiff. Now let the whole forearm drop onto the same key, fingers relaxed, and let the weight do it. The second is louder with less effort, and it is the one that does not injure you.

**Three things, which are really one thing:**

- **Arm weight.** The arm is heavy. Let it fall into the key rather than pushing down with the finger. The finger's job is to hold the shape and transmit the weight, not to generate force.
- **Forearm rotation.** The forearm turns, like a doorknob. Alternating notes — C, G, C, G — are played by rocking it, not by lifting fingers independently.
- **Alignment.** The wrist stays level with the forearm, not bent up and not bent sideways. A bent wrist runs the tendons round a corner, and that is what tendinitis is.

**Why this is lesson two and not lesson fifty.** There is no teacher watching. Tension is invisible to the person producing it, and it compounds: a year of playing with a stiff wrist produces pain that takes months to undo, and focal dystonia takes longer than that. The correction is free now and expensive later.

**The test, which you will use for years.** Stop every few minutes and notice your shoulders. If they have risen, you are holding tension you cannot feel. Drop them, shake the hands out, begin again.

**If anything hurts, stop.** Not "play through it". Pain in the hands, wrists or forearms is information, and with no teacher it is nearly the only kind you get.

**Practice.** Drop the forearm onto one key twenty times, listening for a full sound produced with no effort. Then rock between C and G using rotation only — no finger lifting — slowly, for a minute. Then stop and check the shoulders.
Finding your way around the keys:
The keyboard is one pattern of twelve keys repeated seven and a bit times, and the black keys are what makes it readable.

**The black keys come in groups of two and three.** That is the whole map.

- **C is always immediately left of a group of two.**
- **F is always immediately left of a group of three.**

Everything else follows: D sits between the two blacks, E is to their right, and so on up to B, after which C begins again.

**Find C eleven times** without counting — just by the pattern. Then F. That recognition, not note-naming, is what lets you find a note while reading something else.

**Middle C** is the C nearest the middle of the instrument, usually near the lock or the maker's name on an upright. On your Hoffmann it is the C closest to centre.

**The octave.** The distance from one C to the next. Same letter, same pattern, higher or lower. Play C and the C above together and hear that they are somehow the same note — that is what an octave is, and it is why the letters only go up to G before starting again.

**The black keys have two names each.** The black between C and D is **C♯** (C raised) or **D♭** (D lowered) — the same key, two names, depending on which direction you arrived from. That is not pedantry; it decides how a piece is written and is the whole subject of key signatures later.

**Left is lower, right is higher**, and that corresponds to down and up on the page — which is the one thing about notation that is genuinely intuitive.

**Practice.** Without looking at the keys, find and play every C on the piano. Then every F. Then say the letter of each white key from C to B aloud as you play it, up two octaves and back down.
The fingers have numbers:
A convention that is in every score you will ever read, and takes one minute to learn.

**Both thumbs are 1.** Then 2, 3, 4, 5 outward — index, middle, ring, little. The same numbers in both hands, mirrored, so finger 5 is the little finger on both sides.

**This is not the guitar convention** (where the thumb is T and the index is 1), and not the string convention. If you have seen numbers on music before, these are probably different.

**Why fingering is written at all.** There is usually one sensible way to play a passage with the hand you have, and it is rarely the obvious one. Written fingering is the editor telling you how to arrive at the next bar without running out of fingers — and ignoring it means discovering the problem three bars later.

**Fingering is a decision, not a law.** Editions disagree, hands differ, and a fingering that does not suit your hand is worth changing. But change it deliberately and write it in, because the thing that ruins a piece is using a different fingering each time.

**The weak fingers.** 4 and 5 are weaker and less independent than 1, 2 and 3 — the ring finger shares a tendon with the middle. That is anatomy, not a deficiency to be drilled out, and technique that respects it (rotation, arm weight) works better than technique that fights it. This is the main reason Hanon-style finger-independence drilling is not in this curriculum.

**Practice.** Put your right hand on C D E F G with fingers 1 2 3 4 5, one finger per key. Play each note as a separate arm drop, slowly, saying the number aloud. Then the left hand on the C below, fingers 5 4 3 2 1 on C D E F G. Notice that the thumbs are the two fingers nearest each other.
The five-finger position:
The first thing the hand can actually do: five notes under five fingers, no movement.

**Right hand.** Thumb on middle C, then one finger per white key: C(1) D(2) E(3) F(4) G(5).

**Left hand.** Little finger on the C an octave below middle C, going up: C(5) D(4) E(3) F(2) G(1). Both thumbs end up on G and C respectively — pointing at each other.

**This is a position, not a piece.** The whole point is that the hand does not move, so the only problem is which finger and how. That removes one variable while you learn the other.

**What to listen for, one thing at a time:**

1. **Evenness of volume.** Play 1 2 3 4 5 and listen to whether 4 and 5 are quieter. They will be. The fix is arm weight — leaning the arm slightly towards the little finger — not pressing harder with the finger.
2. **Evenness of timing.** Then listen only to the gaps. 3 to 4 is usually the slow one.

**One fault at a time.** Listening for everything at once means hearing nothing. Volume today, timing tomorrow.

**No metronome yet** — that is the device that clicks a steady beat, and it arrives four lessons from here. Slow and even, by ear, with a pause between notes if you need one.

**The fingers do not lift high.** A raised finger is a tense finger. They stay close to the keys and the arm does the work — the rotation from the previous lesson, applied.

**Practice.** Right hand, C to G and back, ten times, listening only for whether 4 and 5 are as loud as 1 and 2. Then the left hand the same. Then stop and check your shoulders.
Your piano: an old acoustic:
A century-old upright is a particular instrument with particular consequences, and all of them matter for how you learn.

**What it gives you, that a digital does not:**

- **A real action.** Weight, escapement, and resistance that varies across the keyboard. Technique built on this transfers anywhere; technique built on unweighted keys does not, because the fingers never learn to produce a dynamic.
- **Real dynamics.** The difference between a quiet note and a loud one is continuous, not sampled in levels, and your ear learns the whole range.
- **A real pedal** — the right foot's one, which lifts the felt dampers off the strings so notes keep ringing after you let go — including the partial lifts that thin a sound rather than cutting it. Available from the first day; stage 6 is where you learn to use it.
- **It is in the room.** An instrument you walk past gets played. One that needs headphones plugged in does not.

**What it costs:**

- **No headphones**, so practice has a time of day. Work out the hours now rather than discovering them through a complaint.
- **No MIDI.** None of the software that listens to what you played is available — no app that marks a wrong note, no real-time sight-reading feedback. **Your ear and the metronome — the clicking timekeeper from a few lessons' time — are the whole feedback loop.** Every lesson here assumes that.

**Looking after it.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Tuning** | twice a year is standard; once is acceptable. An old piano that has drifted a long way may need two visits to hold pitch |
| **Humidity** | the enemy. 40–60% is the range; extremes crack soundboards and swell actions |
| **Position** | not against an outside wall, not in direct sun, not next to a radiator |
| **The action** | an old upright often has uneven key weight and sluggish repetition. A technician can regulate it, and it is worth more than tuning for playability |

**"Slightly out of tune and not enough to notice" is fine for now** and will stop being fine as your ear improves — which it will, quickly, from the ear-training strand. When you start noticing, that is progress, not a problem.

**Practice.** Find the maker's name and any serial number, usually on the plate inside the top or on the back. Look up roughly when it was made. Then play the lowest A and the highest C and listen to how different the same instrument sounds at its two ends.
Loud and soft, from the arm:
Dynamics are the first musical thing you can do, and they are available before you can read a note.

**How volume is made.** Key speed. A key pressed quickly makes a loud note; slowly, a quiet one. That is the entire mechanism — the hammer is thrown at the string and then free, so nothing you do after the key is down changes the sound.

**Which means pressing harder once the key is down does nothing at all** except create tension. This is the single most common waste of effort at the piano.

**So volume comes from how much arm you drop**, and how fast. More arm, more weight, faster key, louder note. A quiet note is the same movement, smaller and slower, still from the arm — not a stiff finger poking gently.

**The markings**, which you will meet in writing shortly:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **pp** | pianissimo | very quiet |
| **p** | piano | quiet |
| **mp** | mezzo-piano | moderately quiet |
| **mf** | mezzo-forte | moderately loud |
| **f** | forte | loud |
| **ff** | fortissimo | very loud |

They are **relative**, not absolute: *f* in a Mozart sonata is not *f* in a Rachmaninov concerto.

**crescendo** (getting louder) is written *cresc.* or ⟨; **diminuendo** or **decrescendo** is *dim.* or ⟩.

**The instrument is named for this.** "Pianoforte" — quiet-loud — because it could do both, which the harpsichord could not.

**Practice.** Play the five-finger position from *p* to *f* and back, one note per dynamic level, hearing six distinct volumes. Then play all five notes at a steady *p*, listening only for whether any one of them jumps out louder.
A first tune, by hand position:
Something that sounds like music, before any reading. The point is to find out that the instrument makes tunes.

**Ode to Joy**, right hand, entirely inside the five-finger position plus one note.

Finger numbers, in order:

> 3 3 4 5 · 5 4 3 2 · 1 1 2 3 · 3 2 2

> 3 3 4 5 · 5 4 3 2 · 1 1 2 3 · 2 1 1

With the thumb on middle C, that is E E F G · G F E D · C C D E · E D D, and then the same with the ending changed.

**Play it slowly and evenly.** The rhythm is almost all equal notes; the last note of each line is longer. Count a steady 1 2 3 4 under it if that helps.

**What to listen for, one thing only:** whether the notes are **even in length**. The temptation is to rush the easy run down and hold the first note of each group. Listen for the gaps between notes being equal.

**Why this works without reading.** The tune sits under one hand position, so every note is a finger rather than a location, and the hand never moves. That is also why it is a dead end as a method — the next tune will not fit, and that is what stage 2 is for.

**Learn it by ear from here.** Play it until you do not need the numbers, then play it starting on a different note — put the thumb on G and use the same finger pattern. It will sound the same and be in a different key, which is a fact worth meeting now and understanding in stage 4.

**Practice.** Both halves, slowly, until the fingers do it without the numbers. Then from G. Then stop — this is not a piece to polish, it is a demonstration.
Counting, and the metronome:
Rhythm is the half of music that most self-taught players get wrong without knowing, because a wrong note is obvious and a wrong length is not.

**Count aloud.** Not in your head — out loud, from the first week. It is the only reliable way to catch a rhythm being guessed, because the mouth cannot fake a steady pulse the way the inner ear can.

**The beat is not the note.** A beat is a steady pulse underneath; notes last one beat, or two, or half. Tapping your foot while playing is the physical version of the same thing and is worth building now.

**The metronome.** A click at a fixed speed, measured in beats per minute. Free on any phone; a mechanical one is nicer and your piano is the sort of instrument that suits one.

**How to use it, and how not to.**

- **Start far slower than feels necessary.** 60 bpm, one note per click. If it feels absurdly slow it is probably right.
- **Play with it, not after it.** The commonest error is tracking the click a fraction late. Aim to land *on* it, which means hearing the click as the note rather than as a cue.
- **Raise the tempo in small steps** — 4 bpm at a time — and go back down the moment it falls apart.
- **Do not leave it on for everything.** It is a diagnostic, not a crutch. Music does not have a click in it, and playing to one constantly produces rigidity.

**With no recording and no MIDI, the metronome is your second ear.** It is the only objective thing in the room, and it will tell you that the passage you thought was even is not.

**What to listen for.** Put the click on and play the five-finger position, one note per click. Listen only for whether your note arrives with the click or just after it. It will be just after it.

**Practice.** Five minutes with the metronome at 60, playing the five-finger position up and down, counting "1 2 3 4" aloud. Then at 72. Then stop.
Rest, and when to stop:
The lesson that prevents the injury, and the one most likely to be skipped.

**Short and often beats long and rare.** Fifteen to thirty minutes, most days, produces more than two hours on a Sunday — and the research on adult learners is consistent about it. The reason is partly retention and partly that the long session is where tension accumulates.

**Break every twenty to thirty minutes.** Stand up, shake out the hands, let the arms hang. Not a suggestion: fatigue is when technique degrades and when the stiff-wrist habit forms.

**The warning signs, in order of seriousness:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Shoulders risen | tension. Stop, drop them, continue |
| Forearms tired | you are gripping. Stop for the day |
| Tingling or numbness in the fingers | **stop entirely.** This is a nerve sign |
| Pain in the wrist or forearm | **stop, and do not play until it has gone** |

**Pain is not progress.** There is no part of piano technique that requires working through pain, and the belief that there is has ended more playing careers than any other idea in music. If something hurts and keeps hurting, see a doctor who knows about musicians.

**Warm up by playing slowly**, not by stretching aggressively. Cold hands play badly and feel stiff; five minutes of slow five-finger work fixes that.

**The specific risks** for pianists are tendinitis, carpal tunnel syndrome, and focal dystonia — the last being a loss of fine control that is extremely hard to reverse. All three are associated with tension, repetition and poor alignment, which is why the body strand comes before anything else.

**Practising away from the piano is real.** Reading a score, counting a rhythm, and mentally working through a passage all improve playing and cost nothing physically. On a day when the hands are tired, that is what to do.

**Practice.** Set a timer for twenty minutes next time you sit down. When it goes, stand up whether or not you want to. Do that until it is automatic.
The first bars of something you want to:
One piece off the shelf, at the end of stage 1, chosen because wanting to play is the thing that survives.

**Why now, before reading.** Eight stages of exercises with nothing you would choose is how this gets abandoned around stage four. Something you actually want is not a reward for finishing the technical work; it is what makes the technical work happen.

**What fits now.** Right hand melody only, inside a five-finger position or close to it, slow. At this point that means:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Zelda's Lullaby** | slow, few notes, immediately recognisable |
| **Minecraft — Sweden** | simple melody, very forgiving |
| **Gravity Falls** theme | short phrases |
| **Undertale — Snowy** | gentle, repetitive |

**Where to get them.** MuseScore has community arrangements at several difficulties. Search the title, and **filter for the easiest arrangement you can find** — most of them have a "beginner" or "easy" version. These are not public domain, so IMSLP will not have them.

**How to work it, with no reading yet:** find the melody by ear and by finger number, a phrase at a time, exactly as you did with Ode to Joy. A YouTube tutorial with a falling-note display is a legitimate way to learn the notes at this stage, and a bad way to learn to read — which is why stage 2 starts immediately after.

**One phrase a day.** Not the whole thing. A phrase learned properly and played evenly is worth more than the whole tune played approximately, and the approximate version is very hard to unlearn.

**What to listen for:** evenness again. The same fault as everywhere else in this stage.

**Practice.** Pick one. Learn its first phrase — four to eight notes — and play it evenly and slowly twenty times. Then leave it until tomorrow.
What stage 1 was for:
A short review, and the shape of what is coming.

**What should now be true:**

- You sit at the right height, with the shoulders down, without thinking about it.
- You know that the sound comes from the arm, and you can tell when you are pressing with a stiff finger instead.
- You can find any C and any F without counting.
- You know the finger numbers in both hands.
- You can play a five-finger position evenly, slowly, with the metronome at 60.
- You can make six distinguishable dynamic levels.
- You have played a tune and the first phrase of something you chose.
- You stop when something hurts, and you break every twenty minutes.

**What is deliberately not true yet.** You cannot read a staff, you do not know any scales, and you have not used the pedal. All of that is coming and none of it would have been easier first.

**What stage 2 does.** Two strands at once, which is the plan's central decision:

- **Reading** — the grand staff, note values, and playing a written line one hand at a time, counting aloud. Plus sight-reading, which starts in stage 2 and never stops.
- **Chords** — intervals, then triads, then the three or four chords that most songs you want to play are made of.

They are taught together rather than one after the other because they are the two halves of the same thing, and because the pieces you want need both: classical is read, and covers are chorded.

**If any of the list above is shaky**, do that lesson again now. Stage 2 adds a new kind of difficulty — decoding — and adding it on top of an uncertain hand position means failing at two things and being unable to tell which.

**Theory alongside.** Start **Theory 1 · Notation and rhythm** when you start stage 2, at about one theory lesson for every three or four route lessons. The pairing for the whole curriculum is in "How this curriculum works".

**Practice.** Go down the list honestly. Then sit and play the five-finger position, both hands separately, at 60, and listen one last time for whether 4 and 5 are as loud as the rest.
The staff, and why middle C is the hinge:
The grand staff is two staves joined: treble above, bass below. Middle C sits between them, on a short line of its own, belonging to both.

| Clef | Lines, bottom to top | Spaces, bottom to top |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Treble 𝄞 | E G B D F | F A C E |
| Bass 𝄢 | G B D F A | A C E G |

**Do not learn these as mnemonics and stop there.** "Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit" gets you to the note by counting, and counting is what makes sight-reading slow permanently. The goal is recognising a note the way you recognise a letter.

**The way there is landmarks.** Learn four notes absolutely:

- **Middle C** — on its own short line in the gap between the two staves. That short added line is called a ledger line, and the next lesson is about them.
- **Treble G** — the line the treble clef curls around. The clef is a stylised G and it is pointing at it.
- **Bass F** — the line between the bass clef's two dots. The clef is a stylised F.
- **Bass C** — two octaves below middle C, the second space from the bottom.

Everything else is read as a step or a skip **from a landmark**, not counted up from the bottom line.

**The clefs are maps of the same keyboard.** Middle C written in the treble clef and middle C written in the bass clef are the same key. Two staves exist only because one would need an absurd number of ledger lines for the range a piano has.

**Right hand usually reads treble and left hand bass**, and that is a convention rather than a rule — music crosses the hands between staves constantly, and later it will.

**Up on the page is right on the keyboard.** The one genuinely intuitive thing about notation.

**Practice.** On musictheory.net's note identification, treble clef only, ten minutes. Then find the four landmarks on the piano without counting. Do that daily this week.
Ledger lines, and reading outside the st:
The staff holds eleven notes per clef. The piano has 88. Ledger lines are how the other seventy-odd are written.

**A ledger line is a short line added above or below the staff**, continuing the pattern of lines and spaces. Middle C is the first one below the treble staff and the first one above the bass staff — the same note written two ways, which is why it is the hinge.

**Counting ledger lines is slow and everyone does it at first.** The way out is the same as for the staff: landmarks.

- **Two ledger lines above the treble staff** is A.
- **Two below the bass staff** is C — two octaves below middle C.
- Beyond three ledger lines, composers usually give up and write **8va** instead.

**8va and 8vb.** *Ottava* — play an octave higher (above the staff) or lower (below). A dashed line shows how far it applies. **15ma** is two octaves. These exist precisely because four ledger lines are unreadable.

**Why this matters more at the piano than anywhere else.** A violinist reads one clef and a narrow range. A pianist reads two clefs over seven octaves, with the hands crossing between staves. Reading outside the staff is not an edge case here; it is Tuesday.

**The practical approach.** Do not drill ledger lines in isolation beyond the first two above and below. Beyond that, read the shape — "a sixth above the last note" — which is the interval reading the theory track is building.

**Practice.** On musictheory.net, set the note range to include two ledger lines either side and drill ten minutes. Then find and play the notes two ledger lines above the treble staff and two below the bass staff.
Note values, rests, and the beat:
How long a note lasts, which is the half of reading that matters more and gets less attention.

**4/4 in the table means four beats to a bar**, which is the commonest case and gets its own lesson shortly.

| Note | British | American | Beats in 4/4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 𝅝 | semibreve | whole note | 4 |
| 𝅗𝅥 | minim | half note | 2 |
| 𝅘𝅥 | crotchet | quarter note | 1 |
| 𝅘𝅥𝅮 | quaver | eighth note | ½ |
| 𝅘𝅥𝅯 | semiquaver | sixteenth note | ¼ |

**Each is half the one above.** That is the whole system, and it is why the American names are clearer than the British ones.

**Rests mirror them exactly** — a whole rest, a half rest, a quarter rest — and a rest is not a gap in the music. **It is a note of silence with a length**, counted exactly as carefully. Beginners rush rests more than they rush notes.

**Counting.** In 4/4, say "1 2 3 4" aloud. Eighth notes split each beat: "1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and". Sixteenths split again: "1 e and a".

**Count aloud, out loud.** The rhythm you count in your head is the rhythm you already believe; the one you say reveals what you are actually doing.

**Beams.** Quavers and shorter are joined by beams rather than drawn with separate flags, and beams are grouped to show the beat. Four quavers in 4/4 are beamed in twos, not as a four — the beaming is telling you where the beats are, which is a free piece of information most beginners ignore.

**The commonest reading fault is not a wrong note.** It is a note held a beat too long because it was the end of a phrase and felt right. Counting catches it; nothing else does.

**Practice.** Clap and count aloud, at 60 on the metronome: four crotchets; two minims; a semibreve; eight quavers; a crotchet rest followed by three crotchets. Then play the same rhythms on a single note.
Time signatures and bar lines:
The two numbers at the start, which tell you how to count everything after them.

**The top number is how many beats in a bar. The bottom is what kind of note gets one beat.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **4/4** | four crotchet beats. The commonest; also written **C** |
| **3/4** | three crotchet beats. Waltz |
| **2/4** | two crotchet beats. March |
| **6/8** | six quaver beats, felt as two groups of three |
| **2/2** | two minim beats. Also written **¢**, *alla breve* |

**The bottom number is a fraction of a semibreve**: 4 means a crotchet (a quarter), 8 means a quaver (an eighth).

**Bar lines divide the beats into groups** and the first beat of each bar is naturally stronger. That stress is not written anywhere and is part of what makes 3/4 sound different from 4/4 even with identical notes.

**6/8 is the one that catches people.** On paper it is six quavers; in the ear it is two beats, each divided into three. Counting "1 2 3 4 5 6" is correct at slow tempo and wrong at speed, where it is "ONE two three TWO two three".

**Anacrusis — the pickup bar.** A piece can begin partway through a bar, with the first full bar following. The missing beats are usually accounted for at the end. Count the rest of the bar silently before you start, or the piece begins in the wrong place.

**Double bar lines** end a section; a double with two dots is a repeat, which has its own lesson.

**Practice.** Count aloud and clap: two bars of 4/4 in crotchets; two bars of 3/4; two bars of 6/8 felt as two. Then find the time signature of the piece you are learning off the shelf and count a bar of it aloud before playing.
Dotted notes and ties:
Two ways of making a note longer, which look similar and are not.

**A dot after a note adds half its value again.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Dotted minim 𝅗𝅥. | 2 + 1 = 3 beats |
| Dotted crotchet 𝅘𝅥. | 1 + ½ = 1½ beats |
| Dotted quaver 𝅘𝅥𝅮. | ½ + ¼ = ¾ of a beat |

**The dotted crotchet followed by a quaver** is one of the commonest rhythms in music and one of the commonest things played wrongly. Count "1 and 2 and" and play on 1 and on the "and" of 2 — the long note takes a beat and a half, so the short one lands off the beat.

**A tie joins two notes of the same pitch** into one longer note. The second is not played; it is held into.

**A tie is not a slur.** They look identical — a curved line — and mean different things:

- **Tie**: between **two notes of the same pitch**. Hold through.
- **Slur**: over **notes of different pitches**. Play smoothly, which is the articulation lesson.

The pitch tells you which it is, every time.

**Why ties exist when a longer note would do.** Two reasons: a note can be tied across a bar line, where no single note value would fit the counting; and a note can be tied to show the beat structure within a bar, which a dot would obscure.

**Double dots** add half of the half again — a double-dotted crotchet is 1 + ½ + ¼. Rare, and worth recognising.

**What to listen for.** In a dotted rhythm, whether the short note is genuinely short. The usual fault is making it too long, which turns the dotted rhythm into something closer to equal notes.

**Practice.** Clap and count: four bars of 4/4 using dotted crotchet + quaver throughout. Slowly, at 60. Then the same rhythm on one note at the piano.
Reading rhythm before pitch:
A working method for any new piece, and the reason most sight-reading goes wrong.

**The method:**

1. **Look at the time signature and the key signature** — the pair of numbers at the start, and the sharps or flats printed next to the clef. Both have their own lessons; for now, just notice them. Two seconds, and almost everyone skips it.
2. **Clap or tap the rhythm**, counting aloud, without touching the piano.
3. **Say the note names in rhythm**, still not playing.
4. **Then play**, slowly.

**Steps 2 and 3 are the ones that get skipped and they are the ones that work.** Playing immediately means decoding pitch and rhythm and fingering simultaneously, which is three problems at once, and the one that gets dropped is always rhythm — because a wrong note sounds wrong and a wrong length does not.

**Why rhythm first.** A piece played with the right rhythm and some wrong notes is recognisable. A piece with the right notes and guessed rhythm is not music at all. The rhythm is the structure and the notes hang on it.

**Look for patterns before reading note by note.** Most music repeats: the same bar twice, a phrase sequenced a step higher, a rhythm reused. Spotting that a bar is a repeat means not reading it at all.

**Read ahead.** Your eyes should be a beat or more in front of your hands. That feels impossible at first and is the single thing that distinguishes a fluent reader. It is trained by refusing to stop: if you play a wrong note, keep going.

**Never stop to correct.** The instinct to go back and fix is the enemy of reading. It trains stopping, and stopping is the one thing you cannot do when playing with other people or performing.

**Practice.** Take any piece you have not seen — the easiest thing on MuseScore, or a sight-reading sheet. Do steps 1 to 3 without playing. Then play it once, slowly, without stopping for anything.
Your first written line:
Playing from the page, one hand, and the point at which reading becomes real.

**What to use.** Any beginner method book's first pieces, free: Hoffman Academy's downloadable sheets, Furmanczyk's course material, or the easiest arrangements on MuseScore. The specific piece matters far less than the level — it must be easy enough that you are reading rather than decoding.

**Right hand first.** Treble clef, five-finger position, crotchets and minims, in C major so there are no sharps or flats.

**The procedure from the last lesson, every time:** time signature, clap the rhythm counting aloud, say the notes in rhythm, then play.

**Set the hand before you start.** Find the first note, put the hand in position, and know where the fingers are going. Starting to read with the hand in the wrong place guarantees a scramble.

**Count aloud while playing.** Out loud, from now until it is unnecessary — which is much later than it feels.

**What to listen for, one thing:** whether you stopped. Not whether every note was right. Playing through a mistake is the skill; correcting it is a different activity that happens afterwards.

**Then the left hand**, bass clef, the same way. The left hand is slower to read for most people simply because it is read less, and the fix is reading more of it rather than anything clever.

**Do not put them together yet.** That is stage 3, and it is a bigger step than it looks.

**Practice.** Find three easy right-hand pieces. Work one properly by the four steps. Then play the other two through once each without stopping, badly — that is sight-reading, and it starts now.
Sight-reading: the daily ten minutes:
A separate practice from everything else, every day, starting now and never stopping.

**The rules:**

1. **Something you have never seen.** Once it is familiar it is no longer sight-reading.
2. **Well below your playing level.** If it is hard you are not reading, you are decoding. Two grades below is about right.
3. **Do not stop.** Not for wrong notes, not to fix anything, not to go back.
4. **Ten to fifteen minutes, daily.** Consistency beats volume here more than anywhere.
5. **Do not perfect it.** Play it once, move on. Never twice.

**Why rule 3 matters most.** Stopping to correct trains stopping. A sight-reader's job is to keep the music going, and keeping going with a wrong note is strictly better than stopping with a right one.

**Why rule 2 is the one people break.** Sight-reading material should feel almost insultingly easy. The gain is in volume of pages, not difficulty — and this is the exact mirror of the extensive reading argument in any language curriculum.

**Where to get material, free:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **IMSLP** | every beginner collection ever published, out of copyright |
| **MuseScore** | endless community arrangements at every level |
| **Piano Inspires** | 30+ graded sight-reading examples |
| **SightReadly** | five free exercises daily |
| Hymn books, folk collections | hundreds of short, easy, four-part pieces |

**Hymnals are an underrated source**: short, simple, four-part, and there are thousands of them in the public domain.

**The payoff is slow and then sudden.** Four to six weeks of daily practice produces a noticeable change, which is a long time to work with no visible result — and it is the single highest-return habit in this whole curriculum.

**Practice.** Ten minutes. Something new. Do not stop. Tomorrow, something else new.
Sharps, flats and naturals on the page:
The accidentals, and the one rule about them that is always misread.

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **♯** | sharp | raise by a semitone — the next key up, usually black |
| **♭** | flat | lower by a semitone — the next key down |
| **♮** | natural | cancel a sharp or flat |
| **𝄪 / 𝄫** | double sharp / double flat | two semitones. Rare |

**The accidental goes before the note on the page and after the letter in speech.** Written ♯F, said "F sharp".

**The rule that gets misread: an accidental lasts for the rest of the bar**, on that note, in that octave. One ♯ on an F at the start of a bar makes every later F in that bar sharp too, without being written again — and the bar line cancels it.

That is why a natural sign appears seemingly from nowhere mid-bar: it is cancelling something earlier in the same bar.

**The same key, two names.** The black key between C and D is C♯ or D♭ — one key, two spellings. Which one is written depends on the key of the piece and on where the note is going, and it is not arbitrary: C♯ rising to D is a different musical thought from D♭ falling to C.

**E♯ and B♯ exist** and are the white keys F and B. There is no black key between E and F or between B and C, so raising E by a semitone lands on F. This looks like a trick and is a consequence of the keyboard having seven letters and twelve notes.

**The key signature** does the same job at the start of every line, for the whole piece: the sharps or flats printed next to the clef apply to those notes throughout, which is why you do not see ♯ on every F in a piece in G major. Stage 4 is where key signatures are taught properly — "Key signatures on the page" — and until then it is enough to notice them and apply them.

**Practice.** On musictheory.net, drill accidental identification for ten minutes. Then find and play: F♯, B♭, C♯, E♭, A♯. Note which of them are the same key as something else.
The road map of a score:
The symbols that tell you where to go next, which are easy to learn and embarrassing to get wrong.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **𝄆 𝄇** | repeat — play the enclosed section twice |
| **1. / 2.** | first and second time bars — play 1 the first time, skip to 2 on the repeat |
| **D.C.** | *da capo* — go back to the beginning |
| **D.S.** | *dal segno* — go back to the sign 𝄋 |
| **𝄌** | *coda* — jump to the ending |
| **Fine** | the end — where the piece actually finishes after a D.C. |
| **al Fine** | go back and play until *Fine* |
| **𝄂** | final bar line |

**D.C. al Fine** is the commonest: play through, go back to the start, and stop at *Fine* — which is somewhere in the middle.

**D.S. al Coda** is the other: go back to the sign, play until *To Coda*, then jump to the coda.

**Read the road map before playing a piece**, not while. Discovering a D.S. al Coda in performance is how pieces fall apart, and it takes ten seconds to check.

**Repeats are not optional** and are not decoration. A piece with a repeat is a piece whose structure includes the repeat.

**Other markings on the page:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **8va / 8vb** | an octave up or down |
| ***simile*** | carry on in the same manner |
| ***tacet*** | silent |
| **G.P.** | *general pause* — everyone stops |
| **𝄐** | *fermata* — hold, longer than written, as long as feels right |

**The fermata is a judgement, not a duration.** Roughly half as long again is a reasonable default.

**Practice.** Take any piece from MuseScore with repeats in it, and before playing a note, write out the order of the bars as a list. Then play it in that order.
Articulation: legato, staccato, slurs:
How notes are joined or separated, which is most of what makes playing sound musical rather than correct.

**Legato** — smooth, connected. Each note held until the next one sounds, so there is no gap. Marked with a **slur**: a curved line over notes of different pitches.

**The physical technique.** The finger stays down until the next finger is down. There is a moment where both keys are depressed — that overlap is what legato is. Lifting first and then pressing produces a gap however fast you do it.

**Staccato** — short, detached. Marked with a **dot above or below the note**. The note is held about half its written length; the rest is silence.

**Staccato is not loud and not harsh.** It is short. The commonest error is accenting every staccato note.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **·** | staccato — about half length |
| **▾** | staccatissimo — very short |
| **‾** | tenuto — hold the full length, slightly weighted |
| **>** | accent — louder, at the start |
| **^** | marcato — accented and short |

**Slurs also mean phrasing.** A slur over several notes is a musical sentence: slightly stronger at the start, tapering at the end, and a small lift before the next slur begins. That lift is not written and is what makes phrasing audible.

**The default, where nothing is marked**, is somewhere between — connected but not smeared. Baroque music is generally lighter than Romantic music even where neither marks it.

**With no recording to check against, listen for one thing:** whether your legato has gaps. Play a slurred five-note phrase and listen specifically at the joins. There will be gaps, and hearing them is the exercise.

**Practice.** Play the five-finger position legato, then staccato, then legato with a slur over all five and a lift at the end. Listen at the joins. Then find the articulation marks in the piece you are learning and do what they say.
Tempo marks and the Italian:
The words at the top of a score, and the ones sprinkled through it.

**Tempo, slowest to fastest:**

| | | bpm, roughly |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Largo* | broad, very slow | 40–60 |
| *Adagio* | slow, at ease | 66–76 |
| *Andante* | walking pace | 76–108 |
| *Moderato* | moderate | 108–120 |
| *Allegro* | fast, cheerful | 120–156 |
| *Vivace* | lively | 156–176 |
| *Presto* | very fast | 168–200 |

**These are character marks, not metronome marks.** *Allegro* means cheerful as much as it means fast, and the bpm ranges are conventions rather than instructions. A composer who wants a number writes ♩= 96.

**Changing tempo:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *rit.* / *ritardando* | gradually slower |
| *rall.* / *rallentando* | gradually slower (much the same) |
| *accel.* | gradually faster |
| *a tempo* | back to the original speed |
| *rubato* | flexible — stolen time, given back |
| *poco a poco* | little by little |

**Character and manner**, which you will meet constantly:

*dolce* sweetly · *cantabile* singing · *espressivo* expressively · *legato* smoothly · *leggiero* lightly · *grazioso* gracefully · *maestoso* majestically · *sempre* always · *più* more · *meno* less · *molto* very · *poco* a little · *subito* suddenly

**They combine**: *poco a poco accelerando*, *sempre piano*, *più mosso*.

**These are good flashcards** and they go in the deck — a closed set of perhaps sixty words that appear in every score you will ever read.

**Practice.** Find every Italian word in the piece you are currently learning and look up any you do not know. Then play its opening at *largo*, at *andante* and at *allegro*, and notice how much the character changes with nothing else altered.
Intervals under the hand:
The chord strand begins here, and it begins with distance rather than with chords.

**An interval is the distance between two notes**, counted inclusively. C to E is a third: C(1) D(2) E(3).

| Interval | Semitones | A tune that starts with it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minor 2nd | 1 | *Jaws* |
| Major 2nd | 2 | Happy Birthday |
| Minor 3rd | 3 | Smoke on the Water |
| Major 3rd | 4 | When the Saints |
| Perfect 4th | 5 | Here Comes the Bride |
| Tritone | 6 | *The Simpsons* |
| Perfect 5th | 7 | Twinkle Twinkle |
| Minor 6th | 8 | *Love Story* |
| Major 6th | 9 | NBC chimes |
| Minor 7th | 10 | *Star Trek* theme |
| Major 7th | 11 | *Take On Me* (chorus leap) |
| Octave | 12 | *Somewhere Over the Rainbow* |

**Your own reference tune beats the standard one.** If a fifth sounds to you like the Zelda fanfare, use that.

**Major, minor, perfect.** Seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths come in major and minor — one semitone apart, a semitone being the step from one key to the very next, black or white. Fourths, fifths and octaves are "perfect" and have no major or minor form; altered, they become augmented or diminished.

**On the page, an interval is a shape.** Line to the next line is a third. Line to the adjacent space is a second. Reading those shapes rather than naming both notes is the step from slow reading to fluent reading, and it is why this belongs beside the reading strand rather than after it.

**Under the hand, an interval is a span.** A third is "miss one key"; a fifth is thumb-to-little-finger in the five-finger position. The hand learns these as distances and stops measuring them.

**Practice.** Teoria's interval ear training, ten minutes, ascending, up to a fifth. Then play every interval in the table from C and attach your own tune to each.
The major triad:
Three notes, and the foundation of nearly all the music you want to play.

**A major triad is a root, a major third above it, and a perfect fifth above the root.**

C major: **C – E – G**. Count the semitones: C to E is 4, E to G is 3. Four then three — that is the shape of every major triad.

| Chord | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| C | C E G |
| F | F A C |
| G | G B D |
| D | D F♯ A |
| A | A C♯ E |
| E | E G♯ B |
| B♭ | B♭ D F |

**Build them by the semitone count, not by memory.** Four up, then three up. Any root, every time.

**On the staff it is a snowman**: three notes stacked on consecutive lines, or on consecutive spaces. That visual is how chords are read at speed — as a block, not as three notes.

**Under the hand it is 1–3–5** in the five-finger position: thumb, middle, little finger. The hand shape for C major is the hand shape for every major triad; only the position moves.

**Play it as a block and listen.** Then play C–E–G one note at a time. Then play C–E♭–G and hear the difference — that is the minor triad, next lesson, and the gap between them is one semitone and most of the emotional content of Western music.

**Why triads and not something richer.** Almost every song you want to play is built from triads with a few sevenths added. Jazz voicings are not in this curriculum, which means the chord vocabulary you need is genuinely small.

**Practice.** Build and play major triads on C, F, G, D and A, as blocks. Say the three notes aloud as you play each. Then find them written on the staff on musictheory.net's chord identification and drill ten minutes.
The minor triad, and the difference:
One note moves by one semitone and the whole character changes.

**A minor triad is a root, a minor third, and a perfect fifth.** Three semitones then four — the reverse of major.

C minor: **C – E♭ – G**.

| Chord | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Cm | C E♭ G |
| Dm | D F A |
| Em | E G B |
| Am | A C E |
| Fm | F A♭ C |
| Gm | G B♭ D |

**Dm, Em and Am use only white keys**, which makes them the easiest minor chords to find and the reason they turn up constantly in beginner music.

**Only the middle note differs.** C major and C minor share C and G; the third decides. That third is doing nearly all of the work, and noticing it is the beginning of hearing harmony rather than just chords.

**The usual description — major is happy, minor is sad** — is a crude approximation that is good enough to start with and wrong often enough to abandon later. A great deal of minor-key music is not sad, and a great deal of major-key music is.

**Diminished and augmented**, for recognition:

- **Diminished** — root, minor third, **diminished fifth**. C–E♭–G♭. Three plus three. Tense, unstable.
- **Augmented** — root, major third, **augmented fifth**. C–E–G♯. Four plus four. Strange, unsettled.

Both are rarer and both are built by the same semitone counting.

**Chord quality from the shape**, summarised: 4+3 major, 3+4 minor, 3+3 diminished, 4+4 augmented. Four shapes, and the whole of triadic harmony.

**Practice.** Play each major triad from the last lesson, then the minor with the same root, and listen to the third moving. Then find Dm, Em and Am on white keys only. Then drill chord identification on musictheory.net for ten minutes.
Chord symbols, and reading a lead sheet:
The other notation system, which is how every song you want to cover is written.

**A chord symbol is a letter and some modifiers:**

| Symbol | Means |
| --- | --- |
| **C** | C major |
| **Cm** or **Cmin** or **C–** | C minor |
| **C7** | C major triad plus a minor seventh |
| **Cmaj7** or **CΔ** | C major triad plus a major seventh |
| **Cm7** | C minor triad plus a minor seventh |
| **Csus4** | the third replaced by the fourth |
| **Cdim** or **C°** | diminished |
| **C/E** | C major with E in the bass — a slash chord |

**The slash chord is the useful one.** C/E means play C major but put E at the bottom, which is an inversion and is how bass lines move smoothly between chords.

**A lead sheet is a melody with chord symbols above it.** The left hand plays the chords, the right hand the melody, and how you voice the chord is up to you. That freedom is the point and is why lead sheets are shorter than full arrangements.

**This is a second literacy, not a lesser one.** Classical is read from a full score; nearly everything else — pop, hymns, folk, anime arrangements, anything you will accompany — is written as chords. Having both is the plan's central decision and this is where the second one starts.

**Where to find them free:** Ultimate Guitar has chords for nearly every popular song and they work at a piano; hymnals print four-part harmony; MuseScore has both kinds.

**Start with three chords.** A very large number of songs are I, IV and V, which is the next lesson.

**Practice.** Write out the notes of: C, Am, F, G, Dm, G7, C/E. Then find a song you like on Ultimate Guitar and read the chord symbols without playing — just name the notes of each.
I, IV and V — the three chords:
Three chords, and a very large proportion of the music you want to play.

**In C major:** I is **C**, IV is **F**, V is **G** (or **G7**).

**The numbering is by scale degree** — a scale being the ladder of notes a key is built from, and a degree being a note's position on it, counting up from the home note. In C major: C is 1, D is 2, E is 3, F is 4, G is 5. Stage 4 builds all the scales properly; this much is enough to read the numerals.

**So:** The chord built on the first note of the scale is I, on the fourth is IV, on the fifth is V. Roman numerals because the number refers to the position, not the letter — which means the same analysis works in every key.

| Degree | In C | In G | In F |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | C | G | F |
| IV | F | C | B♭ |
| V | G | D | C |

**Why these three.** Between them they contain every note of the scale, and the V chord pulls strongly back to I — which is what makes an ending sound like an ending. That pull is the engine of Western harmony.

**V7 pulls harder.** Adding the seventh (G7 = G B D F) creates a dissonance that resolves to C. Almost every traditional cadence — the chord pair that ends a phrase, and the subject of a stage 7 lesson — is V7 to I.

**vi is the fourth one you need** — A minor in C — and it gives you the four-chord pattern that most pop songs use: **I–V–vi–IV**. In C: C–G–Am–F. That progression carries hundreds of songs, and recognising it is the beginning of playing by ear.

**Lower case for minor.** I, IV, V are major; ii, iii, vi are minor; vii° is diminished. That convention tells you the quality without naming the notes.

**The seven chords of a major key**, which is all you need for most things:

I (C) · ii (Dm) · iii (Em) · IV (F) · V (G) · vi (Am) · vii° (Bdim)

**Practice.** Play C, F, G in the left hand as blocks, slowly, listening to how G wants to return to C. Then C–G–Am–F, four beats each, round and round. Then find a song you know that uses it.
Playing a song from chords:
The first time the chord strand produces music, with nothing read from a staff.

**The simplest accompaniment: block chords.** Left hand plays the chord as a block on beat one of each bar and holds it. Right hand plays the melody.

That is a complete arrangement and it is what every beginner lead sheet expects.

**The shape of a practice:**

1. **Left hand alone**, chords only, in time, with the metronome. Just the changes.
2. **Right hand alone**, melody, from the page or by ear.
3. **Together, slowly** — far slower than the song goes.

**Changing chords is the hard part**, not playing them. The gap while the hand finds the next chord is what breaks the time, and the fix is to **look ahead**: find the next chord's shape before the beat it is needed on.

**Keep the time even when you fluff the chord.** A missing chord with the rhythm intact still sounds like the song; a correct chord that arrives late does not.

**Three songs that are nearly all I–V–vi–IV**, which you can play once you can change between four chords: most of what is on the radio, a great many anime endings, and essentially all campfire guitar music.

**Where the melody comes from.** Either read it from the lead sheet, which is reading practice, or find it by ear, which is ear practice. Both are the point; alternate.

**What to listen for, one thing:** whether the chord changes land exactly on the beat. Put the metronome on and listen only for that. The chord will be late.

**Practice.** Pick a song you like with three or four chords. Left hand, block chords, with the metronome at a slow tempo, until the changes are clean. Only then add the melody.
Broken chords and the first accompanimen:
Block chords are correct and dull. These are the patterns that make a left hand sound like music.

**A broken chord is the same notes, one at a time.** C–E–G instead of all three together. Immediately less heavy, and it fills the bar with movement.

**The patterns worth having:**

| | Pattern | Sounds like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Broken** | 1–3–5–3 | gentle, flowing |
| **Alberti bass** | 1–5–3–5 | classical, Mozart |
| **Arpeggiated** | 1–3–5–8 upward | open, spacious |
| **Root and chord** | bass note, then chord, chord | folk, hymn, waltz |
| **Octave root** | low octave on 1, chord on 3 | pop ballad |

**Alberti bass is worth naming** because you will meet it in every Classical-era sonata — Mozart's C major K.545 opens with it — and because it is the easiest way to make a plain triad move.

**The root-and-chord pattern in 3/4** is the waltz left hand: bass note on beat 1, chord on 2 and 3. Three beats, two different things.

**Choose the pattern for the song.** A ballad wants something slow and open; a march wants root-and-chord; something driving wants straight eighths. The same chords with a different left-hand pattern are a different arrangement.

**Keep it quieter than the melody.** The commonest fault in self-taught accompaniment is a left hand as loud as the right. The left hand is support; it should be a level below. That is an arm-weight decision, from stage 1.

**What to listen for:** the balance between hands. Play the melody and the pattern together and listen only to whether you can hear the tune clearly over it.

**Practice.** Take one chord — C — and play each of the five patterns above for eight bars, with the metronome. Then take a song you know with three chords and play it with a broken-chord left hand.
Inversions, and why chords move smoothly:
The same chord, rearranged, and the thing that makes chord changes stop lurching.

**A triad has three notes, so it has three arrangements:**

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Root position** | C E G | root at the bottom |
| **First inversion** | E G C | third at the bottom — **C/E** |
| **Second inversion** | G C E | fifth at the bottom — **C/G** |

**It is the same chord.** Same three notes, same name, different voicing — voicing being which note of the chord ends up on top and which gets the weight, and a stage 3 lesson of its own — and a different sound, because the lowest note carries most of the weight.

**Why they matter: smooth voice leading.** Changing from C (C E G) to F (F A C) in root position means the whole hand jumps. But C to F/C (C F A) keeps the thumb on C and moves two fingers. The hand barely moves and the change is seamless.

**The rule of thumb: find the nearest version of the next chord.** Between any two triads there is usually a common note; keep it where it is and move the others as little as possible.

**C–F–G–C, voiced smoothly:**

> C (C E G) → F/C (C F A) → G/B (B D G) → C (C E G)

Every change moves one or two fingers rather than the whole hand.

**On the page, an inversion is a chord that is not a snowman.** The notes are no longer on consecutive lines or spaces, which is the visual signal.

**In chord symbols it is the slash:** C/E, C/G, F/A, G/B.

**This is also how bass lines are made.** Choosing inversions to give a stepwise bass — C, B, A, G descending — is the whole technique behind a great many ballads.

**Practice.** Play C major in all three inversions, then F, then G. Then play C–F–G–C twice: once all in root position, once choosing the nearest inversion each time. Listen to the difference in how much the hand moves.
How to learn a new piece:
A method, because approaching a new piece by playing it from the top repeatedly is the slowest way there is.

**1. Read it before touching the piano.** Time signature, key signature, road map, any Italian you do not know. Find the repeats and the structure. Two minutes.

**2. Find the hard bar.** There is always one, and it is where all the time will go. Starting from the beginning every time means practising the easy opening forty times and the hard bar four.

**3. Work in small sections.** Two bars, not a page. A section is small enough when you can hold the whole of it in your head.

**4. Hands separately first**, then together — and together *slowly*, far slower than separately felt comfortable at.

**5. Slowly means slowly enough to be perfect.** The tempo at which you make no mistakes is the correct tempo, and it is usually about half what you want it to be. Practising at a speed where you make errors is practising the errors.

**6. Raise the tempo in small steps** with the metronome. 4 bpm. Drop back the moment it degrades.

**7. Interleave.** When a section is going well, **leave it and do another**, then come back. Drilling one thing to perfection in one sitting produces a result that is gone tomorrow. Alternating feels worse and retains far better — that is the research finding worth building the whole routine on.

**8. Join the sections late.** Practise the joins specifically: the last bar of one section and the first of the next, as its own two-bar fragment. Joins are where learned pieces fall apart.

**The thing to avoid:** playing through from the top for the pleasure of it, and calling it practice. That is playing, which is fine and is not the same activity. Decide which one you are doing.

**Practice.** Take the piece you are learning. Find the hardest bar. Practise that bar alone, hands separately, for five minutes. Then a different section. Then back.
Structuring a session:
What twenty-five minutes should contain, and in what order.

**A workable shape:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **2 min** | sit, check posture, slow five-finger work to warm the hands |
| **10 min** | the piece being learned — one or two sections, slowly, interleaved |
| **10 min** | sight-reading, something new, do not stop |
| **3 min** | the fun piece, or whatever you want to play |

**Interleaved** means rotating between sections and skills rather than drilling one to completion. It feels worse and retains better; stage 3 makes the case.

**Warm up by playing slowly, not by stretching.** Cold hands are stiff and play badly; five minutes of slow work fixes it, and aggressive stretching before playing is more likely to cause trouble than prevent it.

**Sight-reading goes in the middle, not the end**, because the end is where it gets dropped when time runs out — and it is the thing that most needs daily contact.

**End with something you enjoy.** Not sentiment: the last thing in a session is what you remember about it, and what you remember determines whether you sit down tomorrow.

**Break every twenty to thirty minutes** if the session is longer. Stand, shake the hands out.

**On a day with ten minutes**, do sight-reading. On a day with five, do the fun piece. The worst session is the one that does not happen because the full routine felt impossible.

**Two short sessions beat one long one.** Twenty minutes in the morning and twenty in the evening is better than forty in one block, because of how consolidation works between sessions.

**A day off is fine.** Several in a row is where habits die, and the way back in is a five-minute session rather than a resolution to do better.

**Practice.** Do one session today by the shape above, with a timer on each part. Notice which part you wanted to skip — that is the one to protect.
A piece from the page:
The end of stage 2: something off the shelf, read rather than learned by numbers.

**What fits now.** Right hand melody from notation, left hand block chords or a simple broken pattern, in C major or close to it, slow.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Zelda's Lullaby** | slow, few chords, famous |
| **Minecraft — Wet Hands** | mostly broken chords, very forgiving |
| **Howl's Moving Castle — Merry-Go-Round** | the easy arrangement; the hard one returns later |
| **Undertale — Home** | gentle, repetitive, simple harmony |

**On MuseScore, filter for the easiest arrangement.** Most popular pieces have several, from beginner to concert, and the difficulty of the arrangement is the only difficulty that matters. These are not public domain, which is why IMSLP will not have them.

**Work it by the method from two lessons ago.** Read it first, find the hard bar, sections, hands separately, slowly, interleaved.

**Expect it to take a fortnight**, not an evening. The first real piece always does, and the second takes half as long.

**Use both strands.** Read the melody from the staff; name the chords in the left hand as chord symbols. If the arrangement writes out the left hand note by note, work out what chord each bar is — that is where the two halves of this stage meet, and it is the habit that makes the rest of the curriculum coherent.

**What to listen for:** balance. Can you hear the melody clearly over the left hand? Probably not, at first — the left hand is almost always too loud.

**Practice.** Choose one. Read it through first. Learn the first eight bars properly over a week. Do not move on until those eight are even, in time, and balanced.
What stage 2 was for:
Review, and the shape of stage 3.

**Reading — what should now be true:**

- You find notes on the staff by landmark rather than by counting.
- You know the note values and can count a bar aloud in 4/4, 3/4 and 6/8.
- You read rhythm before pitch, every time, on a new piece.
- You can play a written line, one hand, slowly, without stopping.
- You have done ten minutes of sight-reading on most days — and this is the one most likely to have slipped.

**Chords:**

- You can build any major and minor triad by semitone count.
- You know I, IV, V and vi, and the I–V–vi–IV pattern.
- You can read chord symbols and play a song from a lead sheet.
- You can play block chords, broken chords and an Alberti bass.
- You know what an inversion is and why it makes changes smoother.

**And:** you have learned one piece off the shelf, properly, from the page.

**What stage 3 does.** Hands together — which is the real difficulty of the instrument and the point at which most people stall. Two independent lines at once, and then the dynamics and phrasing that turn correct notes into music.

It is a bigger step than it looks, and the reason is cognitive rather than physical: each hand alone is a solved problem, and doing both is a third problem that neither solved.

**Before moving on.** Every item on the lists above should be comfortable, not merely possible. Stage 3 adds a difficulty of a new kind, and adding it on top of shaky reading means failing at two things and being unable to tell which.

**Theory alongside.** Finish **Theory 1 · Notation and rhythm** during stage 3. It is the notation you have just been using, in full.

**Practice.** Go down both lists. For anything you hesitated on, go back to that lesson this week. Then play your stage 2 piece once, slowly, and listen to the balance.
Why hands together is hard:
The point most people stall at, and it is worth knowing why before failing at it.

**The difficulty is not physical.** Each hand alone is a solved problem. Doing both is a third problem that neither solved, and the reason is attention: you have one, and it cannot be in two places.

**What actually happens.** You play hands together, and one hand goes on automatic while you attend to the other. When the attended hand hits something hard, the automatic hand stops — because it was never automatic, only unattended.

**So the goal is not "concentrate harder".** It is to make one hand genuinely automatic, which means it has to be over-learned on its own first, well past the point where it feels learned.

**Hands-separate practice is therefore not a stepping stone to be hurried through.** It is how a hand becomes automatic. The usual error is doing it until each hand is *possible* and then combining, which combines two unreliable things.

**The second reason it is hard: the hands want to synchronise.** Both hands naturally do the same thing at the same time — clap, grip, lift. Independent lines fight that, which is why parallel motion is easy and a left hand in a different rhythm is not.

**The order that works:**

1. Both hands doing the **same thing** at the same time.
2. Both hands doing the **mirrored** thing.
3. One hand **still**, the other moving.
4. Both moving, **same rhythm**, different notes.
5. Both moving, **different rhythms**.

That is the order of this stage, and each step is a genuine increase.

**Go slower than feels necessary.** Hands together at half the speed of hands separately is normal, not a failure.

**Practice.** Play your five-finger position with the right hand while the left hand holds a single low C. Then swap. Notice how much attention the holding hand still takes.
Parallel motion:
Both hands playing the same thing at the same time — the easiest case, and the one to get genuinely clean before anything else.

**The exercise.** Right hand C D E F G from middle C; left hand C D E F G from the C below. Same finger numbers at the same moment: 1-2-3-4-5 in the right, 5-4-3-2-1 in the left.

Both hands play C with different fingers, then D, then E. Same letters, same rhythm, same direction.

**What to listen for, and only this: are the hands actually together?** They are almost certainly not. One leads by a fraction — usually the right, because it has the melody and gets the attention.

**How to hear it when you cannot hear it.** Play one note — both hands' C together, once — and listen for whether it sounds like one attack or two. A doubled note with a tiny gap has a distinctive flam to it. If you can hear a flam on one note, you will hear it in a passage.

**The metronome helps here more than anywhere.** Set it slow and listen for whether the click, the left hand and the right hand are one sound or three.

**If one hand is consistently late**, it is the hand with less attention. Deliberately attend to the late one for a few repetitions and it usually fixes itself.

**Then octaves apart in the same direction**, which is the same exercise and sounds fuller.

**Why bother with something this simple.** Because "together" is a standard you are setting now, and a tolerance for a slight flam at this stage becomes a permanent feature of your playing. It is far easier to insist on it with five notes than with a Chopin nocturne.

**Practice.** Five-finger position, parallel, both hands, at 60, for two minutes. Listen only for the flam. Then at 72. Then stop.
Contrary motion:
The hands moving in opposite directions, which is easier than it sounds and teaches something parallel motion cannot.

**The exercise.** Both thumbs on middle C — right hand thumb on middle C, left hand thumb on the same middle C or the C below. Now move outward: right hand up C D E F G, left hand down C B A G F. Same fingers at the same moment, opposite directions.

**Why it is easy.** The fingers are doing the same thing — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 outward in both hands. The hands are mirror images, and mirroring is something the body does naturally.

**Why it is useful.** It separates the finger pattern from the direction, which is the first step towards the hands doing genuinely different things. And contrary motion scales — which stage 4 reaches — are the easiest scales to play hands together for exactly this reason.

**What to listen for:** the same flam as in parallel motion. Contrary motion often exposes it more clearly because the two lines diverge and stop masking each other.

**Then the harder version:** same direction, different fingers. Right hand 1-2-3-4-5 going up while the left hand also goes up, 5-4-3-2-1. Now the hands are moving together but the fingers are not mirrored, and the brain has to do two things.

That is the real step, and it is noticeably harder than either of the first two.

**The order matters.** Parallel first because it is one instruction. Contrary second because it is mirrored, which is also nearly one instruction. Same-direction-different-fingers third, because it is genuinely two.

**Practice.** Contrary motion five-finger, at 60, two minutes, listening for the flam. Then both hands ascending together — right 1-2-3-4-5, left 5-4-3-2-1 — and notice how much harder it is.
One hand still, one moving:
The first genuinely independent thing the hands do, and a direct preparation for melody-with-accompaniment.

**The exercise.** Left hand holds a single low C and keeps holding it. Right hand plays the five-finger position, up and down, evenly.

**The difficulty is not in the moving hand.** It is that the holding hand wants to join in — to lift when the other lifts, to press again on a strong beat. Keeping a hand still while the other works is a real skill and is the thing accompaniment is built on.

**Then the other way:** right hand holds a note, left hand plays the pattern. This is harder, because the left hand is less practised and now has the attention-demanding job.

**Then: one hand holds a chord.** Left hand holds C–E–G as a block while the right hand plays the melody above it. That is already a complete texture and is how a great many simple arrangements work.

**What to listen for:** whether the held note or chord gets re-struck or released early. It should sound continuously under the moving line. With a sustaining acoustic you will hear it decay naturally, which is correct — what is wrong is lifting.

**Then: the held hand changes.** Left hand holds C for four beats, then F for four, then G, then C, while the right hand plays a scale-ish line over the top. Now one hand is changing slowly while the other changes quickly, which is the actual shape of most music.

**This is where the chord strand and the hands-together strand meet.** The left hand holding I, IV, V under a right-hand melody is a song.

**Practice.** Left hand holds low C, right hand plays five-finger up and down four times. Then the left hand changes: C, F, G, C, one per four beats, right hand continuing. Listen for whether the left hand changes exactly on the beat.
Melody over block chords:
The first real two-hand texture: a tune in the right hand, chords underneath.

**The shape.** Right hand plays the melody. Left hand plays the chord of the bar as a block, on beat one, and holds it.

**Work it in this order, every time:**

1. **Left hand alone** — just the chord changes, in time, with the metronome. Over-learn this until it needs no attention.
2. **Right hand alone** — the melody, from the page or by ear, until it is fluent.
3. **Together, at half speed.**

**Step 1 is the one that gets skipped**, and it is the one that makes the rest possible. The left hand must be automatic, because the attention is going to the melody.

**The change is the hard part, not the chord.** Practise the changes alone: C to F, four beats each, with the metronome, until the hand finds the next shape before it is needed. Then C to G. Then the actual sequence.

**Look ahead with the left hand.** The hand should be moving towards the next chord while the current one is still sounding.

**Balance: the melody must be louder.** A left hand as loud as the right is the single commonest fault in self-taught playing, and it is an arm-weight decision — more arm into the right, less into the left. Play a bar and listen only to whether the tune is clearly on top.

**It will not be.** Everyone's left hand is too loud at first, because it is playing three notes to the melody's one and three notes are louder than one.

**What to listen for, one thing per session.** Session one: do the chords land on the beat? Session two: can you hear the melody over them? Not both at once.

**Practice.** Take a song with three chords. Left hand alone until it is automatic. Right hand alone until it is fluent. Then together at half tempo, listening only for the balance.
Melody over broken chords:
The same texture with the left hand moving, which is harder and sounds far better.

**The step up from block chords.** The left hand now plays four notes a bar instead of one, so it is no longer "set it and forget it" — it has its own rhythm, running under a different rhythm in the right hand.

**Start with the simplest pattern**: 1–5–3–5 (Alberti) or 1–3–5–3, one note per beat, against a melody in longer notes.

**The order of difficulty:**

1. Melody in **whole notes** over a moving left hand. Easiest — the right hand barely does anything.
2. Melody in **quarter notes**, one per left-hand note. Both hands move together, which is parallel motion again.
3. Melody in a **different rhythm**. The real thing.

**Work through them in that order** rather than attempting (3) directly.

**The trap.** When the melody gets hard, the left hand pattern slows down or stumbles. That is the automaticity problem from the first lesson of this stage, and the answer is more hands-separate work on the left — not more hands-together repetitions.

**A good test of automaticity:** can you play the left-hand pattern while saying something out loud? If talking stops it, it is not automatic yet.

**The left hand is still quieter.** A broken-chord accompaniment is even easier to overplay than a block chord, because it is moving and movement draws attention.

**With the pedal** this texture becomes much richer, and that is stage 6. For now, no pedal — the fingers must do the connecting.

**Practice.** Hold a C major chord as 1–5–3–5 in the left hand, one note per beat, at 60, for a minute, until it runs by itself. Then play a simple melody over it in long notes. Then shorten the melody's notes.
Two different rhythms:
The hardest thing in this stage: each hand in its own rhythm at the same time.

**Start with the simplest case** — one hand playing twice as fast as the other. Left hand on beats 1 and 3, right hand on 1, 2, 3, 4. Every left-hand note coincides with a right-hand note, so the hands meet regularly.

**Then: three against two is not yet.** That belongs in stage 6 and attempting it now produces frustration rather than skill.

**The method that works: find where the hands coincide.**

Any two rhythms line up at certain points. Mark those points. Between them, play the faster hand and let the slower one fall where it falls. The coincidences are the anchors.

**Count aloud, and count the faster hand.** If the right hand has quavers, count "1 and 2 and"; the left hand's crotchets land on the numbers. Counting the slower hand means guessing the faster one.

**Hands separately, with the counting, first.** Then together at a tempo so slow it is almost absurd — the point is to let the brain see where each note goes, which it cannot do at speed.

**The "block it out" technique.** Play both hands' notes for one beat as a chord, all together, then the next beat, then the next. That removes the rhythm entirely and shows you which notes coincide. Then restore the rhythm.

**What to listen for:** whether the hands stay independent or collapse into each other. The usual failure is the slower hand drifting to match the faster one.

**Do not rush this.** Rhythmic independence is the thing that takes longest and it develops over years, not weeks. A simple piece played with genuinely independent hands is worth far more than a hard one played with them glued together.

**Practice.** Left hand crotchets, right hand quavers, on a single note each, at 60, counting "1 and 2 and" aloud. Two minutes. Then with the five-finger position in the right hand.
Balance: making the melody speak:
The thing that most distinguishes playing that sounds musical from playing that sounds correct.

**The problem.** Both hands are attached to the same person, and whatever you do to one you tend to do to the other. Playing the melody louder means consciously playing the accompaniment quieter, and the second instruction is the one that gets lost.

**It is an arm-weight decision, not a finger one.** More arm into the melody hand; less arm, lighter drop, into the other. Trying to play quietly by tensing the fingers produces a thin, uneven sound and a sore hand.

**The test.** Play a bar and ask: if someone walked past the room, what would they hear? If it is a wash, the balance is wrong. The melody should be the thing you notice and everything else should be underneath it.

**The exaggeration exercise.** Play the accompaniment much too quietly — absurdly quiet, almost not sounding — with the melody at a normal level. That feels wrong and is usually about right. Then bring the accompaniment up slightly.

**Within one hand**, the same problem exists. A right hand playing melody and inner harmony has to bring out the top note, which is done by leaning the hand slightly towards the little finger. That is voicing, and it is the next lesson.

**Why this matters more on your piano than on a digital.** An acoustic has a far wider dynamic range and a much more sensitive action, so the difference between balanced and unbalanced is more audible. That is an advantage: the instrument is telling you the truth.

**What to listen for, the only thing this session:** can you hear the tune clearly above everything else? Nothing else matters until that is yes.

**Practice.** Take any piece you can play hands together. Play it with the left hand absurdly quiet. Then bring it up until the balance sounds right, and notice how quiet that still is.
Voicing within one hand:
Bringing out one note of a chord while the others stay underneath — the next level of control after balance between hands.

**Where it comes up.** A right hand playing a melody with harmony beneath it, which is most hymns, most chorales, and a great deal of piano writing. The top note is the tune; the notes under it are accompaniment played by the same hand.

**The technique.** Lean the hand slightly towards the finger that must sound. For a top-note melody, tilt the hand towards the little finger so more of the arm's weight arrives there. The other fingers play with less.
