**Why a player needs it.** Phrasing — where to breathe, where to shape to, where to take time — follows the phrase structure exactly. A pianist who can name the structure plays it; one who cannot plays bar by bar.

**Practice.** Take the first sixteen bars of a Classical piece you can play. Mark the phrases, name the cadence at each end, and decide whether it is a period or a sentence. Then play it with a breath at each phrase end.
The standard forms:
A reference list of how pieces are shaped, with what each implies for learning and playing one.

**Strophic.** The same music repeated with different words. Songs, hymns.

**Binary — AB.** Two sections, each usually repeated. The first ends in the dominant or the relative major, the second returns home. Baroque dances: minuets, gavottes, sarabandes.

**Rounded binary — A B A′**, with the first section repeated and the B and A′ repeated together. The commonest short classical shape, and it is the minuet without its trio.

**Ternary — ABA.** Three distinct sections with a real return. Character pieces, nocturnes, and the minuet-and-trio as a whole, where the trio is the B.

**Rondo — ABACA**, or ABACABA. A recurring refrain with contrasting episodes. Finales, and light pieces.

**Sonata form.** Exposition, development, recapitulation, as stage 8 described. First movements, and often finales.

**Sonata-rondo** mixes the two, with the refrain functioning as the first theme.

**Theme and variations.** A theme, then altered statements of it. Whole movements and whole pieces.

**Fugue.** A texture and a procedure rather than a fixed form, from the counterpoint module.

**Through-composed.** No repetition of sections. Some Romantic songs and much modern music.

**Verse–chorus, with a bridge.** Pop, anime, film songs. Intro, verse, chorus, verse, chorus, bridge, chorus, out.

**The multi-movement shapes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Suite** | a set of dances, usually in one key — Baroque |
| **Sonata cycle** | fast, slow, dance, fast — three or four movements |
| **Concerto** | three movements, with an orchestra |
| **Song cycle** | a set of songs with a thread |
| **Prelude and fugue** | a pair, as in the Well-Tempered Clavier |

**What knowing the form buys you when learning a piece**, which is the practical point: the repetitions tell you how much material there actually is. A rounded binary with both repeats is roughly half as much music as its page count suggests, and a sonata movement's recapitulation is largely learned when its exposition is.

**And when writing**, from stage 10: the form is the plan, and ABA with an altered return is the one that reliably works.

**Practice.** Take three pieces you can play and name the form of each, with its bar counts. Then look at how much of each piece is literally repeated material.
Score reading:
Reading music written for more than one instrument. It comes up in accompanying, in studying, and in arranging.

**How a score is laid out.** One system per group of staves, read top to bottom, with the instruments in a fixed order: woodwind at the top, then brass, then percussion, then any soloist or voices, then strings at the bottom. Within each family, highest instrument first.

**What makes it hard for a pianist**, and there are three things:

1. **Many staves at once**, so the eye has to scan vertically through a page.
2. **Transposing instruments**, which sound a different pitch from the one written. The next lesson.
3. **C clefs** — the viola reads alto clef, and cello, bassoon and trombone read tenor clef in their upper registers.

**How to read one usefully**, without learning to conduct:

- **Find the bass line.** Cellos and basses, at the bottom of the strings. That gives you the harmony.
- **Find the melody**, which is usually the first violins or a solo instrument, and may move.
- **Ignore the rest on a first pass.** Doubling, inner parts and accompaniment figures are detail.
- **Then read the harmony vertically** at the strong beats.

**Which is exactly reading by harmony** from stage 7, applied to a bigger page.

**Short score and open score.** A short score condenses the parts onto two to four staves; an open score gives every part its own. Vocal music often appears in open score — four staves for four voices — and reading that is a specific skill, closer to reading four separate parts than reading piano music.

**Piano reductions** are the practical version: an orchestral work arranged for two hands. Useful for study, and they are what accompanists play.

**Why learn any of this.** To accompany a singer from a vocal score, to play from a hymnal in open score, to study a piece you are not going to play, and to arrange orchestral or band music for the piano — which requires reading the score to know what is actually in it.

**Where to practise.** IMSLP has full scores of everything. Start with a string quartet — four staves, no transposing instruments, two C clefs — then a Classical symphony, which is the gentlest orchestral case.

**Practice.** Find a string quartet movement on IMSLP. Read the cello line alone for eight bars. Then read the first violin and cello together. Then name the harmony at each bar's first beat.
Transposing instruments:
Why a trumpet part and the sound it makes are different notes, and how to deal with it.

**The convention.** Many wind and brass instruments are built in a key other than C, and their music is written so that the player's fingering is consistent. A clarinet in B♭ reading a written C sounds a B♭ — a tone lower.

**Why it exists.** A clarinettist owns instruments in B♭ and A and plays both with the same fingerings; the transposition lives in the notation instead of in the player's hands. It is a convenience for the player and a nuisance for everyone else.

**The common ones:**

| Instrument | Written C sounds | Transposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clarinet in B♭ | B♭ | down a major 2nd |
| Trumpet in B♭ | B♭ | down a major 2nd |
| Horn in F | F | down a perfect 5th |
| Alto saxophone (E♭) | E♭ | down a major 6th |
| Tenor saxophone (B♭) | B♭ | down a major 9th |
| Cor anglais (F) | F | down a perfect 5th |
| Piccolo | an octave up | up an octave |
| Double bass, guitar | an octave down | down an octave |

**Strings, flute, oboe, bassoon, trombone and tuba are usually in C** — written pitch is sounding pitch.

**The two directions you may need:**

1. **Score to sounding pitch**, when reading a score or working out the harmony. Transpose the written note down by the interval in the table.
2. **Sounding pitch to part**, when writing for someone. Transpose up by the same interval, and adjust the key signature.

**The key signature follows.** A piece in C major gives a B♭ clarinet a part in D major — two sharps. That is why band music is written in flat keys: it keeps the wind parts in easy ones.

**What this means practically for you:**

- **Accompanying a trumpeter or clarinettist**: their part is not in your key. Either they transpose, or you do, or you use a piano part written for the combination.
- **Arranging for a friend who plays one**: write their part transposed, or they will not be able to read it.
- **Reading scores**: horn parts in F are the ones that will confuse you most, and the classical convention of writing horns without a key signature makes it worse.

**The practical shortcut** when playing with one person: ask what their sounding pitch is, and transpose their written part by eye — which is the transposing-at-sight exercise from stage 8, with a real use.

**Practice.** A clarinettist's part is in D major. What key does it sound in? Then write a C major scale as it would appear in a B♭ trumpet part. Then find a horn part in a Classical score and work out its sounding pitch.
The overtone series:
Why instruments sound different from each other, why some intervals are consonant, and why a piano's tuning is a compromise. One physical fact underlies all of it.

**A vibrating string does not vibrate only at one frequency.** It vibrates along its whole length, and also in halves, thirds, quarters and so on, all at once. Each of those produces a pitch.

**The series, from a fundamental of C two octaves below middle C:**

| Partial | Pitch | Interval above the fundamental |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | C | the fundamental |
| 2 | C | octave |
| 3 | G | perfect 12th — a fifth above the octave |
| 4 | C | two octaves |
| 5 | E | major 10th |
| 6 | G | |
| 7 | B♭-ish | noticeably flat of the written B♭ |
| 8 | C | three octaves |
| 9 | D | |
| 10 | E | |
| 11 | F♯-ish | between F and F♯ |

**Three consequences, and they explain a great deal:**

1. **Timbre is the mix of partials.** A piano, a violin and a flute playing the same note differ in which partials are strong and how they decay. That mix is what you recognise as the instrument.
2. **Consonance follows simple ratios.** The octave is 2:1, the fifth 3:2, the fourth 4:3, the major third 5:4. The simpler the ratio, the more partials the two notes share, and the more consonant the interval sounds. That is why the fifth and octave are the "perfect" intervals and why the system is built on them.
3. **The seventh and eleventh partials do not fit the keyboard.** They lie between the notes of our scale, which is why the series cannot simply be used as a scale.

**Sympathetic resonance, which stage 6 described**, is this fact at work: lifting the dampers lets strings whose fundamentals match the partials of the note you played vibrate too. The piano's richness with the pedal down is the overtone series made audible.

**It also explains the major triad.** Partials 4, 5 and 6 are C, E and G — a major chord, present inside every single note. The major triad is not a cultural choice; it is in the physics.

**And it explains brass instruments**, which play the series directly by overblowing — which is why a bugle can only play certain notes, and why horn parts in Classical music are limited to them.

**Practice.** Hold the sustain pedal down and play a low C sharply, then release the key and listen for the pitches above it. Then play a low C and, without pedal, press the keys of G and E above it silently — then play the low C and hear them ring.
Temperament and tuning:
Why twelve equal semitones is a compromise, what the alternatives were, and what the Well-Tempered Clavier was arguing about.

**The problem.** Pure intervals do not fit into octaves. Stack twelve pure fifths of 3:2 and you overshoot seven octaves by a small amount — the Pythagorean comma, about a quarter of a semitone. So something has to be bent, and every tuning system is a decision about what.

**Just intonation** keeps intervals pure in one key, and the comma piles up elsewhere. Beautiful in that key, unusable in others, and impossible on a fixed-pitch instrument that must modulate.

**Pythagorean tuning** stacks pure fifths and accepts bad thirds. Medieval, suited to music built on fifths and fourths.

**Meantone temperament** narrows the fifths slightly to get good major thirds. The standard for Renaissance and early Baroque keyboards; it has a "wolf" interval somewhere, which the player avoids by staying in nearby keys.

**Well temperaments** — several, and Werckmeister's is the best known — distribute the error unevenly so that every key is usable and the common keys are better than the remote ones. Each key has a slightly different character as a result.

**Equal temperament** divides the octave into twelve exactly equal semitones. Every key is equally usable and equally slightly impure: fifths are very slightly narrow and major thirds noticeably wide of pure. It is the universal modern standard and it is what your piano is tuned to.

**What *The Well-Tempered Clavier* was for.** Bach wrote preludes and fugues in all twenty-four keys to demonstrate that a well-tempered instrument could play in all of them. The title is a claim about tuning. It is sometimes read as advocating equal temperament; the scholarship mostly says well temperament rather than equal, and the precise system he used is not settled.

**What this means for your piano.** It is in equal temperament, so enharmonic notes are literally identical, every key is equally in tune, and the slight impurity of thirds is a property of the system rather than of your instrument. What is a property of your instrument is that it has drifted — which is tuning, not temperament.

**The other tuning facts worth knowing:**

- **A440** is the modern standard pitch, and it has risen over centuries. Baroque pitch was commonly around A415 — about a semitone lower — which is why historically informed recordings sound flat against your piano.
- **Stretch tuning**: piano tuners deliberately tune the extremes slightly wide, because the strings' overtones are not perfectly harmonic. Your piano is not tuned to mathematically equal temperament and should not be.
- **Beating** is what you hear when two notes are nearly in tune, and it is what a tuner listens for.

**Practice.** Play a major third low on the keyboard and listen for the slight beating — that is equal temperament's wide third. Then play a fifth and notice it is much cleaner. Then listen to a harpsichord recording in meantone and hear the difference in the thirds.
Analysis as a habit:
The last lesson of the theory track, and the one that puts all of it to work: a single procedure, applied to everything you learn.

**The procedure, which is stage 7's eight steps with the track's vocabulary added:**

1. **Name the key**, from the signature and the final cadence.
2. **Mark the form** — the sections, their bar numbers, their keys, and what each does.
3. **Mark the phrase structure** inside each section: phrases, periods or sentences, and every cadence named.
4. **Write the chord of each bar** as a letter, then as a Roman numeral with its inversion figure.
5. **Label the non-chord tones** in any bar where the harmony looked ambiguous.
6. **Mark the modulations**, with the pivot chord's two functions written one above the other.
7. **Circle the chromatic chords** and name each: secondary dominant, borrowed, Neapolitan, augmented sixth, chromatic mediant, passing.
8. **Look at the bass line alone.** Walking, leaping, pedal point. Is it a melody?
9. **Look at the melody alone.** Its shape, its high point, its motif and what is done to it.
10. **Then the practical layer**: fingering, pedalling by harmony, the dynamic plan, the near-identical passages.

**Half an hour per piece**, and it does not need the instrument.

**What it returns**, which is the argument for making it a habit:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Memory** | an analytical memory survives interruption; a muscular one does not |
| **Phrasing** | follows the cadences, directly |
| **Pedalling** | follows the harmony, directly |
| **Learning speed** | repeated material is learned once |
| **Difficult bars** | often become easy once understood as one object |
| **Writing** | every analysis is a lesson in how a piece is made |
| **Reading** | recognised shapes are read as shapes |

**Do it before learning, not after.** The return is highest on the first day and declines; an analysis done after the piece is learned fixes nothing that was learned wrongly.

**Keep the marked scores.** They are the reason a revived piece comes back in days, and they accumulate into a record of what you understand.

**Where the theory track ends.** It has given you the notation in detail, the scales and keys systematically, harmony as a written discipline, counterpoint and voice-leading, and the physical basis of why any of it sounds like it does. That is more than the route needs and roughly the content of a conservatoire's first-year theory. What is past it — species counterpoint in full, Schenkerian analysis, twentieth-century set theory, orchestration — is available free online if you ever want it.

**What to do with all of it: use it on the next piece.** Theory that is not applied to music is trivia, and theory applied every time becomes invisible, which is the point.

**Practice.** Take the piece you are learning now and run all ten steps on it, with a pencil, away from the piano. Then play it and notice what changed.
Reducing a score to two hands:
Turning music written for other forces into a piano piece. It is the practical end of score reading and it is how a great deal of the repertoire you already play came to exist.

**What a reduction has to decide.** An orchestra has dozens of lines and you have ten fingers, so the question is not how to fit it all in but what the music actually is.

**The priority order:**

1. **The bass line.** Always. It carries the harmony and it is the one part that cannot be left out.
2. **The melody**, wherever it is and whichever instrument has it — and it moves.
3. **The harmony**, as a compact filling between them.
4. **The rhythm**, if a part of the texture is rhythmically characteristic.
5. **Counter-melodies**, if a hand is free. Usually one is not.
6. **Everything else**, which is left out.

**The specific decisions:**

- **Octave doublings go.** An orchestral tutti doubles everything at several octaves; a piano needs one or two.
- **Sustained inner notes become pedalled or implied.** Strings can hold a chord for eight bars; a piano cannot, so you either re-strike, arpeggiate, or let the pedal carry it.
- **A repeated-note string texture becomes repeated chords**, a tremolo, or a broken-chord figure.
- **Register matters more than note count.** The same chord low is mud; spread wide with a gap above the bass it sounds like an orchestra.
- **Wind and brass chords become block chords**, usually in the right hand, usually with the fifth dropped.

**Transposing instruments must be read at sounding pitch** before anything else. A reduction made from the written notes of a horn part will be a fifth wrong.

**Then make it playable.** A reduction that needs three hands is a study score, not a piano piece. Redistribute between hands, drop notes, and simplify figures until it works — and the test is playing it, not looking at it.

**Where this is useful**: arranging band or orchestral music you like, making a practical accompaniment from an orchestral score, arranging a film or game cue that only exists as a recording, and understanding why published piano arrangements make the choices they do.

**The related skill is arranging from a recording**, which is the same decisions with no score to read — stage 9's ear work plus this lesson's priorities.

**Published reductions are worth studying.** Liszt's transcriptions of Beethoven's symphonies are the extreme case and are free; vocal scores of operas are the everyday case, and they are models of what to keep.

**Practice.** Take a short orchestral passage from IMSLP — a Classical symphony's opening is ideal. Write a two-hand reduction of eight bars: bass, melody, minimal harmony. Then play it and simplify whatever does not work.
How this curriculum works:
Read this one first. It is the only lesson that is about the curriculum rather than about the piano.

**The stages are an ordered route and nothing more.** No dates, no pacing, no gates. Do them in order, move on when something is genuinely solid, repeat a lesson as often as you like. Eleven stages, and stage 11 does not end — *ad astra*.

**Every lesson teaches its point in full and then tells you what to practise.** You should never have to open a source to learn the thing the lesson is about. The sources listed on a lesson are there if you want more of it, or a video of someone's hands doing it, or the score.

**Any term is explained where it is first used.** If a word turns up that you do not know and the lesson does not explain it, that is a fault in the lesson — the theory track is where the full definition lives, and the cards carry the ones worth memorising.

**The theory track runs alongside the stages**, drawn as its own row of cards beneath the stage deck. It is not optional extra reading and it is not a later project; it is the reference half of the same curriculum. Here is what pairs with what:

| Theory module | Run it during | Why then |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Theory 1 · Notation and rhythm** | stages 2–3 | you are learning to read, and this is the notation in full |
| **Theory 2 · Scales, keys and intervals** | stage 4 | stage 4 plays the keys; this one explains the system behind them |
| **Theory 3 · Harmony on paper** | stage 7 | stage 7 is harmony by ear and at the keyboard; this is harmony written down |
| **Theory 4 · Counterpoint and voice-leading** | stage 8 | the Bach stage. Four-part writing and the chorales belong beside it. |
| **Theory 5 · Form, score and sound** | stages 8–10 | long pieces, then writing your own, both of which need form |

**The rate: one theory lesson for every three or four route lessons**, or one a week — whichever you will actually do. They are short and they are reading rather than playing, so they fit where practice does not.

**Stage 1 needs no theory module.** Start Theory 1 when you start stage 2.

**Three habits run underneath everything, each separate from the lesson you are on:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Sight-reading** | ten minutes a day, from stage 2 onwards, forever. Material below your playing level. It is the first thing to lapse and the highest-return habit here. |
| **The cards** | the gold card above the stage list opens the deck — terms, chord spellings, key signatures, fingerings. Ten new a day, and the rest is review. |
| **Ear training** | ten minutes, away from the piano. Formally a stage 9 habit; start it whenever you like. |

**The practice session shape** is in stage 1's "Structuring a session", and a longer version is in stage 11. Twenty-five minutes is a session; ninety is a good one; five minutes is better than nothing.

**Stop rules matter more than any of this.** Pain, tingling, numbness or a tight forearm means stop for the day. Stage 1 covers posture and tension, stage 6 covers it again for the technical work, and nothing in this curriculum is worth an injury.

**Practice.** Open the theory track and read the first lesson of Theory 1 — not now, but when you reach stage 2. Then come back here and start "Sitting at it".
